e:
Derived from ecdysis, the biological process of shedding or molting.
From Ancient Greek ekdúsis (“a stripping off, shedding”), via English ecdysis (“molting; shedding of an outer layer”).
Coined by H. L. Mencken from ecdysis (“moulting”) (on the model of enthusiast etc.).
q: I had never seen an ecdysiast before; toward the end she was wearing nothing but seven beads, four of them sweat.
1973, Kyril Bonfiglioli, Don't Point That Thing at Me, Penguin, published 2001, page 79:

However, the Queen of Ecdysiasts, Gypsy Rose Lee, was not amused. In a 1940 interview, she leveled her guns against Mencken: "Ecdysiast, he calls me! Why, the man... has been reading books! Dictionaries! We don't wear feathers and molt them off... What does he know about stripping?"
2004, Chrysti the Wordsmith, Verbivore's Feast: A Banquet of Word and Phrase Origins, Farcountry Press, page 107:

e: From ecdysis (“shedding, moulting”) (from Ancient Greek ἔκδυσις (ékdusis, “stripping”)) + steroid.
q: The ecdysteroid group includes more than 250 polyhydroxysterols that occur in plants and animals, with 20-hydroxyecdysone (20-OH-E) being the physiologically active moulting hormone in most insects (Lafont 2000).

2007, Guy Smagghe, “12: Insect Cell Lines as Tools in Insecticide Mode of Action Research”, in Isaac Ishaaya, Ralf Nauen, A. Rami Horowitz, editors, Insecticides Design Using Advanced Technologies, Sp

In some dipteran species, ecdysteroids synthesis starts at almost the same time as the onset of vitellogenin synthesis, whereas in other species like orthopterans the synthesis starts only towards the end of vitellogenin uptake.
2008, John L. Capinera, editor, Encyclopedia of Entomology, 2nd edition, Springer, page 1279:

Ecdysteroids in crustaceans differ substantially from those of their fellow arthropods, the insects. Crustacean ecdysteroids and ecdysteroid nuclear receptors are similar to those of insects, but differ in the number of hormones and in the number and structure of the receptor isoforms.
2009, Penny M. Hopkins, “Chapter 3: Crustacean Ecdysteroids and their Receptors”, in Guy Smagghe, editor, Ecdysone: Structures and Functions, Springer, page 73:

e: Via French ecdotique from Ancient Greek ἐκδοτικός (ekdotikós), relating to ἔκδοσις (ékdosis, literally “outgiving”) which amongst other things means “publishing”.

q: Ovarian ecdysiotropic hormones, a testes ecdysiotropin, and ecdysiostatins produced by neurosecretory cells of the brain modulate ecdysteroid production by these organs.
2010, Marc J Klowden, Physiological Systems in Insects, page 29:

e: From Ancient Greek ἔκδυσις (ékdusis, “stripping”), from ἐκδύω (ekdúō, “I take off”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + δύω (dúō, “I get in”).
